sections.body_md:
An incremental gradient method splits an objective into a sum of blocks and spends the gradient of one block at a time. After each block the parameter moves, and the next block is evaluated at the new point. A batch step does the opposite: it sums every block gradient at the same point and only then moves. At a finite step the two updates are different algorithms, and the order of the blocks matters.

The cost of the incremental pass is that a constant step length need not converge to a stationary point of the sum. On a pair of quadratics the endpoint of a repeated pass can settle at a point where the full gradient is still nonzero. That settled point slides toward a stationary point only as the constant length tends to zero. The usual way to reach a stationary point is therefore a step that tends to zero while the sum of the lengths stays infinite: the vanishing length kills the bias, and the infinite sum still lets the iterates travel.

A batch gradient step on a smooth function has a different budget. If the length stays below twice the reciprocal of a Lipschitz constant, the gradient norms tend to zero with no need to drive the length to zero.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
One block updates
\[
x:= x - t \nabla f_i(x)
\]
and the next block sees the new \(x\). A batch step uses \(\sum_i \nabla f_i\) at a single point.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take the blocks \(\tfrac12(u - 9)^2\) and \(\tfrac12(u - 19)^2\), start at \(14\), and use length \(0.4\), with the first block first. The first gradient is \(5\), so the point moves to \(14 - 2 = 12\). The second gradient at \(12\) is \(-7\), so the point moves to \(12 + 2.8\).

The crate reading is 14.8. The full gradient there is \(1.6\), not zero. A batch step would have summed both gradients at \(14\) before moving, and it would not have produced this point. Another pass, started at \(14.8\), evaluates its first gradient at \(14.8\) rather than at \(14\).

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Evaluating every later block at the original point is a batch step written one term at a time. The incremental pass is defined by the update in between. A second slip is to expect a constant length to land on the minimizer of the sum. The endpoint of a repeated pass can sit where the full gradient is not zero. A third is to enlarge the length in the hope that one pass will finish the problem. A longer constant step can sit even farther from a stationary point. A fourth is to forget that the order of the blocks changes the intermediate points whenever the length is finite.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Recursive least squares does not minimize each new block by itself. A length-1 pass that jumps to the newest center forgets the earlier blocks and stops there. The recursive step minimizes the old quadratic together with the new block, and one Gauss-Newton step is exact because the stacked cost is quadratic. A nonlinear block is linearized at the current estimate before that stacked step.
